t: Binary String With Substrings Representing 1 To N
o: We must decide whether every integer from 1 to n has its standard binary form (no leading zeros) appearing somewhere as a contiguous substring of s. In Example 1, s = "0110" contains "1" (for 1), "10" (for 2), and "11" (for 3), so the answer is true. In Example 2, "100" (binary of 4) never appears in "0110", so the answer is false. The crucial constraint interplay: s has at most 1000 characters while n can be up to 10^9 (~30 bits). That means s contains at most about 1000 × 30 = 30000 distinct binary substrings of length at most 30, so we cannot iterate over all n values naively for large n — instead we should enumerate what s *does* contain and compare against {1, ..., n}.
k: Any valid binary representation of a number in [1, n] has at most floor(log2 n) + 1 bits, so only substrings of s up to that length matter.
s has length ≤ 1000, so there are at most ~30,000 candidate substrings — enumerate them rather than testing all n numbers.
A substring starting with '0' represents no valid integer (no leading zeros allowed), so skip zero-valued prefixes.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force substring search per number
a.i: The most direct idea: for every integer i in [1, n], compute its binary string and search for it inside s using built-in substring search. This is correct because it directly mirrors the problem definition. However, with n up to 10^9 this does up to a billion searches over a 1000-character string, which will time out on worst-case inputs — it is included as the conceptual baseline that motivates the optimal approach.
s: For each i from 1 to n, format i in base 2 without leading zeros.
Search for that binary string in s using an efficient built-in find.
If any i's representation is missing, return false.
If all are found, return true.
a.t: O(n · |s| · log n) — for each of n numbers we run a substring search costing roughly |s| · log n; infeasible when n is near 10^9.
a.sp: O(log n) — temporary storage for one binary string at a time.

a.n: Approach 2: Enumerate substrings of bounded length (optimal)
a.i: Flip the direction of checking: instead of asking for each number whether it occurs, collect every integer value represented by a substring of s whose length is at most the bit-length of n (longer substrings exceed n or start with useless leading zeros). Since |s| ≤ 1000 and the max useful length is ≤ 30, this examines at most ~30,000 windows. If the resulting set has exactly n elements, and all values are in [1, n], then every number 1..n was found — equivalently, just check that the set size equals n since duplicates collapse and out-of-range values are skipped.
s: Compute L = n.bit_length(), the maximum useful substring length.
For each start index i in s, extend a rolling value x left-to-right: x = 2*x + bit.
Stop extending when the window length exceeds L or x exceeds n.
Add x to a set whenever x >= 1 (skip leading-zero prefixes that evaluate to 0).
Return true iff the set's size equals n, meaning all of 1..n were represented.
a.t: O(|s| · log n) — each of the |s| start positions extends at most log2(n)+1 characters, with early termination once the value exceeds n.
a.sp: O(min(|s| · log n, n)) — the set holds at most ~30,000 distinct values, also bounded by n.

w: In an interview, state the brute force first to show you understand the problem, then immediately point out that n can be 10^9 while |s| ≤ 1000, and pivot to enumerating substrings of length at most bit_length(n). Common pitfalls: forgetting that binary representations have no leading zeros (a substring like "01" does not represent 1 — though the inner '1' alone does), off-by-one in computing the maximum bit length (use n.bit_length() or equivalent), and overflowing 32-bit intermediates in Java/C++ when building values before the > n check (use 64-bit or break promptly). Edge cases: n = 1 requires only that s contain a '1'; s consisting of all zeros always returns false for any n ≥ 1. A likely follow-up: what if s could be much longer — then you would build a suffix automaton or suffix array of s and test each of the n binary strings in O(log n) each, giving O(n log n) total.
